Although education for patients and caregivers is acknowledged as a crucial element in the management of AD, conventional approaches, such as workshops or in-person consultations, are often resource intensive and face challenges related to scalability, personalization, and relapse prevention. Digital tools present promising alternatives; however, empirical evidence supporting their effectiveness in young children is currently limited. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate whether a smartphone-based patient-caregiver educational program could reduce relapse rates in children aged 0 to 6 years with moderate-to-severe AD, compared with conventional outpatient consultation alone. Methods: In this multicenter, randomized, parallel-controlled trial, 615 children were enrolled across 12 tertiary pediatric dermatology centers in China and randomized (1:1) to receive either a smartphone-based digital education program with standard care (intervention group) or conventional face-to-face consultation only (control group). The 12-week digital https://www.jmir.org/2026/1/e79559 J Med Internet Res 2026 | vol. 28 | e79559 | p. 1 (page number not for citation purposes) JOURNAL OF MEDICAL INTERNET RESEARCH Yang et al program, delivered via the WeChat-based Skin Care E-Station platform, included structured multimedia modules, interactive educational materials, and a dynamic electronic action plan tailored to the child’s age and disease stage. The primary endpoint was the 12-week relapse rate after the acute treatment phase. The secondary endpoints included changes in disease severity (Scoring Atopic Dermatitis, Peak Pruritus Numerical Rating Scale, and Patient-Oriented Eczema Measure) and quality of life (Children’s Dermatology Life Quality Index or Infant’s Dermatitis Quality of Life Index and Dermatitis Family Impact) up to 52 weeks. Results: Among 615 randomized participants (mean age 3.3, SD 1.7 y; n=317, 51.5% male), relapse at 12 weeks occurred significantly less frequently in the digital education group than in the control group (16.6% vs 24.0%; relative risk 0.69, 95% CI 0.50‐0.96; P=.02). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed superior relapse-free survival over the first 100 days (hazard ratio 0.688, 95% CI 0.490‐0.966; P=.03). Differences in relapse rates beyond 12 weeks and in secondary outcomes were not statistically significant. Engagement tracking indicated high adherence to the intervention, with 58.0% of caregivers maintaining regular weekly use of the digital platform. Conclusions: A structured smartphone-based patient-caregiver educational intervention significantly reduced short-term relapse risk among young children with moderate-to-severe AD, likely through improved caregiver recognition and early management of disease flares. Although effects diminished beyond 12 weeks, this approach demonstrates that scalable digital education is a feasible and effective adjunct to standard care in pediatric AD. Future research should focus on sustaining engagement, optimizing long-term reinforcement, and assessing cost-effectiveness in diverse caregiver populations. JSON: Name: smartphone_eczema_education_rct Title: Randomized controlled evaluation of a smartphone-based multimodal caregiver education program to reduce short-term relapse in pediatric atopic dermatitis Short Hypothesis: A 12-week smartphone-based multimodal caregiver education program delivered in addition to standard outpatient care causes a lower 12-week relapse rate (SCORAD increase ≥10 from end-of-acute phase) in children aged 0–6 years with moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis compared with standard outpatient care alone. Related Work: Prior approaches to caregiver education for pediatric atopic dermatitis include face-to-face counseling, nurse-led consultations, workshops/eczema schools, printed handouts, and standalone multimedia (video or web) interventions. These methods demonstrate short-term benefits in symptoms, adherence, and caregiver coping but are constrained by limited scalability, high personnel and facility costs, and variability in content standardization. Existing digital efforts (video tutorials or simple apps) improve accessibility but often lack interactivity, dynamic tailoring, and integrated clinician access; evidence from randomized trials in very young children (0–6 years) and trials powered for relapse prevention is limited. Common unresolved issues include sustained engagement over months, disentangling which digital features (multimedia modules, tailored action plans, or on-demand clinician access) drive clinical benefit, incomplete long-term outcome data, limited cost-effectiveness analyses, and potential exclusion of digitally underserved populations. Abstract: Atopic dermatitis in young children frequently follows a relapsing course; caregiver recognition and early management of flares can reduce morbidity and health care use. We propose a randomized controlled evaluation of a smartphone-based multimodal caregiver education program, combining frequent brief multimedia modules, a dynamically tailored electronic action plan, and an on-demand clinician consultation channel, delivered alongside standard outpatient care. The primary aim is to test whether this intervention reduces 12-week relapse rates (defined by SCORAD increase ≥10 after an acute-phase treatment) versus standard care alone. Secondary aims include time-to-relapse, longitudinal changes in clinical severity (SCORAD, POEM, PP-NRS), caregiver-reported quality of life, platform engagement metrics, and health care utilization up to 52 weeks. The main contribution is a mechanistic, multi-arm trial design that isolates the effects of core digital components (modules vs modules+clinician access) and quantifies short-term relapse prevention and engagement dynamics. Expected impact: evidence on scalable digital education features that reduce early relapses in pediatric atopic dermatitis and guidance for deployment and optimization in routine care. Experiments: Study design: multicenter, three-arm, parallel, randomized controlled trial with 1:1:1 allocation. Population: children 0–6 years with moderate-to-severe AD (SCORAD ≥25, IGA ≥3) who complete a standardized 2-week acute-phase treatment and whose primary caregiver can read Chinese and use WeChat. Sample size: 900 randomized (300 per arm) to detect an absolute 8% difference in 12-week relapse rate between arms with 80% power, two-sided α=0.05, and assumed 25% control relapse, allowing 25% attrition. Arms: (A) standard outpatient care (control); (B) smartphone modules + tailored EAP delivered 3×/week for 12 weeks; (C) same as B plus on-demand encrypted clinician consultation (“green channel”). Datasets collected: baseline demographics, SCORAD, IGA, POEM, PP-NRS, CDLQI/IDQOL, DFI, platform logs (logins, time on content, module completion), medication use, unscheduled visits, and adverse events; follow-up at weeks 4, 8, 12, 24, 36, 52. Baselines for comparison: control arm and within-intervention ablation (B vs C). Additional substudy: randomized frequency ablation within arm B (3×/week vs 1×/week) for n=150. Primary outcome: 12-week relapse rate (binary). Secondary outcomes: time-to-relapse (days), trajectory of SCORAD/POEM/PP-NRS/QoL to 52 weeks, engagement metrics, number of unscheduled visits, topical steroid/TAC ointment usage, and cost per relapse averted. Evaluation metrics: absolute and relative risk, risk difference, Cox proportional hazards (HR), Kaplan-Meier survival, GEE for repeated continuous outcomes (Gaussian identity, robust SEs), per-protocol and ITT analyses, multiple imputation for missing data (MICE, m=10). Statistical tests: chi-square for binary outcomes, log-rank and Cox for time-to-event, Wald tests for model coefficients, and pre-specified subgroup analyses by age strata (0–2 vs 3–6 years) and baseline SCORAD tertiles. Ablation/comparison studies: (1) B vs C to isolate effect of clinician access; (2) B 3×/week vs B 1×/week to test dose-response on engagement and relapse; (3) per-protocol restricted analysis comparing high-engagement (≥weekly completed modules) vs low-engagement participants. Data monitoring: interim analysis at 50% enrollment for futility and safety (O'Brien-Fleming boundaries). Risk Factors and Limitations: Selection bias toward caregivers with smartphone proficiency and WeChat access limits generalizability to rural or digitally underserved populations. Differential attrition and engagement decay over time may bias long-term outcome estimates. Self-reported measures and photo-based remote SCORAD assessments risk measurement error and misclassification of relapse. Contamination between arms (caregivers sharing content) may reduce effect size. Dependence on a single platform (WeChat) and third-party CRO raises data governance and platform-availability risks. Real-time clinician access (arm C) has scalability and workforce cost constraints, which may limit external implementation. Statistical power assumptions may be inaccurate if actual relapse rates differ from estimates. Regulatory and privacy requirements may restrict data linkage needed for health care utilization or cost-effectiveness analyses. Findings may not generalize to different languages, cultural contexts, or health systems with different baseline care pathways.
